title_tag: 华盛顿对华鹰派‘复仇’成功：黄仁勋出局，芯片出口管制要加码了？ —— 美国《华盛顿邮报》外刊讲解第1229天
h1: 华盛顿对华鹰派‘复仇’成功：黄仁勋出局，芯片出口管制要加码了？
category: 美国《华盛顿邮报》外刊讲解 第1229天

headline.en_html: Behind Jensen Huang’s spy scandal, a shadow war for Trump’s ear on China
headline.zh: 华盛顿对华鹰派‘复仇’成功：黄仁勋出局，芯片出口管制要加码了？

paragraphs.en_html: As Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang gained extraordinary access to President Donald Trump and secured his blessing to sell artificial intelligence chips to China, he fueled a backlash among Washington officials and national security hawks who wanted to keep the powerful technology out of Beijing’s hands. Some national security officials within the Trump administration chafed at Huang’s influence over the president, according to two former officials.

Huang’s downfall, which has the potential to mark a dramatic shift in power, was ultimately set in motion by one of the capital’s most influential China hard-liners, national security adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Rubio issued a memo warning Trump about the relationship between Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, based on a report generated by the CIA, according to a person familiar with the matter. When the findings of Rubio’s memo — swiping at one of Trump’s closest allies — leaked in news reports, they set off a chain of events that culminated in Huang’s resignation Thursday.

Huang admitted to and apologized for having an affair with an executive at an Nvidia customer, who American spies suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board launched an investigation, but Huang ultimately resigned following reports of another affair with a subordinate. After Huang’s resignation, Trump referred to him as a “legend” who had “done a fantastic job.” At a Group of Seven summit in Paris this week, Rubio declined several times to answer reporters’ questions on his role in alerting the White House to Huang’s affair.

The ouster marks a huge victory for those who had long sought to curb Huang’s influence over Trump’s policy toward Beijing, and a stunning turn in a shadow battle that has raged for years between Nvidia and those in Washington who see China as a military and technology threat. Until recently, Huang’s close relationship with Trump appeared to give him the upper hand. But with the downfall of the leatherjacket-sporting CEO, the hawks are ready to seize on the moment to redirect the national agenda toward tougher policies on China.

Many of Trump’s national security team had not shared the president’s view on exports of chips, according to a former official who worked on chips policy and is still connected to the industry, who likened Huang’s relationship to handing officials a “nuclear bomb.” “They wanted to destroy the influence Jensen had over the president,” said the former official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal dynamics. “Things are forever changed,” said Fedasiuk, a longtime advocate for controls on chip exports.

For decades, Nvidia’s computer chips powered the graphics in video games and were not a matter of national security. But for many in Washington, that began to change at the start of the AI boom and what officials in the Biden administration saw as the dawn of a new contest with China poised to reshape the two nations’ military and economic power. Huang took a different view, arguing that chipmakers should be able to continue to sell into China, hooking them on American systems in a way that would ultimately benefit the U.S.

In December, when Trump said he had green-lit exports of a new class of chips, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the bargain had been hammered out between Huang and the president. “So it’s the great American technologist talking to the great businessman president, and they reached what they thought was the right answer for this particular moment,” Lutnick told CNBC. A Trump appointee at the Commerce department bureau responsible for export licenses expedited Nvidia’s chip applications, according to two former agency officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid professional retaliation.

Huang advocated for his position in sometimes caustic terms. In an interview with a podcast in September 2025, he said the term “China hawk” should be a badge of shame. “They think they’re doing the right thing for our country, but it’s not patriotic,” he said. “Not even a little bit.” Staff at Washington think tanks and on Capitol Hill responded by designing badges designating them China hawks that they passed around among themselves. At the time, Eric Sayers, a managing director at consulting firm Beacon Global Strategies, posted to social media that the group had “long memories” — a message he shared again in recent days as the scandal around Huang deepened.

Now, with Huang sidelined — and Republican committee chairs planning to haul him in to provide information about the affair — the sponsors of a trio of new measures say they are increasingly optimistic that they can push them through as part of an annual defense bill. The bills would place export restrictions on the most powerful AI chips, require technology in chips to detect smuggling and limit Chinese access to chipmaking equipment. “Leading up to this moment, we were waiting to see who Nvidia deploys to kill these bills,” said a Senate Democratic aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal strategy. “Now all this stuff has come out, it puts them in a very, very tough position.
